intro: Janáček ends his three-part rhapsody with the Cossack leader’s capture, execution and defiant prophecy. Short phrases collide in the orchestra before organ and bells carry the music towards its great closing hymn.

sections.label: A · Strings and winds exchange fragments
C · Muted horns and string runs
Coda · Organ and repeated string phrases

cues.title: Fragments across the orchestra
cues.text: Cellos hurry through short runs while bassoons and horns answer in clipped phrases. The music passes between strings and winds, with plucked notes interrupting the bowing. Janáček marks the opening Con moto — with movement.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice full score, 1927, corrected reprint 1947, pp. 61–64: Con moto opening, cello figures, bassoon and horn phrases, and pizzicato strings. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/24/IMSLP129624-PMLP43971-Janacek_-_Taras_Bulba_-_I._The_Death_of_Andrei.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gogol in Brno
cues.text: In 1905 Janáček hears Gogol’s story read in Russian at the Russian Circle in Brno. Ten years later, during the First World War, he begins this rhapsody. Its three movements follow the deaths of Taras’s two sons and then their father.
cues.evidence: Moravian Museum’s Janáček catalogue, Taras Bulba, JW VI/15: the Russian Circle reading in 1905, composition in 1915 and revision in 1918, and the three movement titles. https://www.leosjanacek.eu/en/orchestral/

cues.title: A brisk dance
cues.text: The Presto brings short wind phrases over a brisk accompaniment, with snare drum and plucked strings. Repeated notes keep the dance moving while the instruments exchange their little scraps of melody.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, corrected reprint 1947, pp. 73–76, bars 52–86: Presto in 2/8, snare drum, pizzicato strings and repeated woodwind phrases. Timing follows the broad score passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Muted horns and strings
cues.text: The music retreats into muted horns and scurrying strings. Small pauses separate their phrases. The horns hold their notes while the strings pass quick runs between the violas and cellos.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, corrected reprint 1947, pp. 83–84, bars 129–140: the quiet horn phrase after the Maestoso, followed by Tempo I, muted horns and strings, and alternating viola and cello runs. Timing follows the broad score passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The organ returns
cues.text: The coda is marked Andante. The organ broadens the orchestra’s chords while the strings keep repeating a short phrase. Janáček builds the closing hymn from these insistent repetitions.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, corrected reprint 1947, pp. 89–92: Coda, Andante, organ chords and repeated string figures; Malcolm Rayment’s HMV sleeve notes identify the organ’s return at the coda. Timing follows the broad score passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Maestoso, with bells
cues.text: The organ holds broad chords, and bells sound over the strings’ repeated notes. Janáček marks this passage Maestoso — majestically — then relaxes the pace again to Meno mosso.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, corrected reprint 1947, pp. 93–94, bars 191–197: Maestoso with bells, organ and repeated string notes, followed by Meno mosso. John Tyrrell discusses this passage in “Janáček’s maestoso”, p. 30: https://www.hippocampus.si/ISBN/978-961-7023-72-5/978-961-7023-72-5.23-49.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Taras at the stake
cues.text: Gogol’s Taras is captured and condemned to burn. He dies predicting his people’s victory. Janáček makes that prophecy the destination of the movement: the long closing pages summon organ, brass and bells.
cues.evidence: Malcolm Rayment’s notes on the original HMV ALP 1675 sleeve describe the capture, execution and prophecy, and the organ and bells in the coda. https://archive.org/download/lp_taras-bulba-les-fresques_leos-janacek-bohuslav-martinu-the-royal/lp_taras-bulba-les-fresques_leos-janacek-bohuslav-martinu-the-royal_djvu.txt

cues.title: The last broad chords
cues.text: The final paragraph broadens to Grave. Brass, organ and bells reinforce the closing chords, with the strings holding their high notes above the bass.
cues.evidence: Hudební matice score, corrected reprint 1947, pp. 100–103: sustained string notes, ritardando and final Grave with brass, bells and organ. Timing follows the broad closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The original sleeve names Rafael Kubelik and the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. Czech diacritics are restored in the display name. The organist and other individual players are unidentified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The LP identifies the third movement as side 1, band 3. The exact score edition and orchestral parts used by Kubelík are unknown. Notes use the Hudební matice score of 1927 in its corrected 1947 reprint. Section and cue times are approximate score-proportion passages, guided by the recording’s broad changes; they have no bar alignment or aural review. No track concatenation or excerpt trimming is used.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Thierry Vagne’s discography dates the HMV Taras Bulba sessions to 10 and 12 April 1958, printed as 4/10,12/1958. The selected movement’s allocation to a particular session or take is unknown. The 1959 date on the original sleeve is first publication, not recording.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The consulted sleeve, transfer metadata and discography do not establish the recording venue. The record company’s Hayes address and the Archive’s Cebu transfer location are separate from the performance session.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Janáček’s underlying composition is public domain under ordinary life-plus-70 terms.
fields.note: Janáček died on 12 August 1928. Taras Bulba was first published as a piano-duet arrangement in 1925 and as a full orchestral score in 1927. This assessment concerns the composition; unidentified modern editorial additions have separate rights.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis: lawful commercial publication in 1959, before 1963.
fields.note: The original HMV ALP 1675 sleeve explicitly states “Recording first published 1959”. Its former 50-year phonogram term expired before the extension applying to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013. The selected source uses eu-published-before-1963 with published: 1959. Internet Archive supplies no Creative Commons licence. US recording status is not established, and this territorial basis is not worldwide clearance.

composer.epithet: He wrote down the voices of strangers in Brno, then gave opera some of its most painfully recognisable people.
facts: Chorister in Old Brno; organ studies in Prague; conservatories in Leipzig and Vienna
Founded the Organ School in 1881; directed it until 1919
Nine operas, two string quartets, Sinfonietta, Glagolitic Mass, piano music and folk-song collections
composer.background:
In August 1865, Janáček’s mother took her eleven-year-old son to Brno and left him at the Augustinian monastery. His father, a schoolmaster in Hukvaldy, was ill; the family needed the scholarship. Nearly sixty years later, in his autobiographical sketch of 1924, Janáček remembered “a hard bed, harder bread. No caresses.” The monastery’s choirmaster, Pavel Křížkovský, taught him music. The boy sang at services, went to concerts and the theatre, and learned the profession that would keep him in Brno for the rest of his life.

He trained as a teacher, studied at the Prague Organ School, and tried the conservatories in Leipzig and Vienna. Prague also gave him a lasting friendship with Dvořák. Back in Brno he taught, conducted the Beseda choir and organised concerts; in 1881 he founded the Organ School, which he directed until 1919. His programmes included Beethoven’s Missa solemnis and Dvořák’s Stabat mater. The composer who would eventually make an orchestra speak in sharp, unfinished sentences spent much of his working life rehearsing other men’s long ones.
